recordTitle: If two consecutive positive integers are powerful, must at least one be a perfect square?
recordStatementVerbatim: If two consecutive positive integers are powerful, must at least one be a perfect square?

recordFieldsVerbatim.Current status:
Solved
Proof contributors: Solomon W. Golomb (counterexample in [Go70], 1970; [attribution source](https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/365)).

recordProvenance.reviewNoteVerbatim: Disproved: 12167 = 23³ and 12168 = 2³ × 3² × 13² are consecutive powerful numbers, and neither is a perfect square. A powerful number has exponent at least two in every prime factor. The displayed factorizations verify this property for 12167 and 12168. Both lie strictly between 110² = 12100 and 111² = 12321, so neither is a square. This disproves the stated yes/no question. This record covers that question only, not the separate counting question in [Erdős problem #365](https://www.erdosproblems.com/365). The previous 1976→2026 interval is removed because it does not establish the duration of the stated question.

formalizedStatement: There exist consecutive positive integers n and m = n + 1 (both >= 1) that are both powerful and neither of which is a perfect square. The verifier accepts the explicit pair as its input and checks (i) m = n + 1, (ii) every prime divisor p of n and of m satisfies p^2 | the number, (iii) neither n nor m is a square. The published pair of the record is 12167 and 12168.
formalizationCarrier: the T1 verifier input contract (spec-powerful-pair.py fields n, m) and the witness node's provenance quote

definitions.recordReading: the record's own review note: "A powerful number has exponent at least two in every prime factor"
definitions.formalizedReading: for every prime p, p | x implies p^2 | x
definitions.note: Equivalent definitions agree; the exponent form is what the verifier certifies.

definitions.recordReading: "two consecutive positive integers" in the question
definitions.note: The pair is unordered in the record; the task fixes the smaller member as n.

definitions.formalizedReading: there is no integer k with k^2 = x
definitions.note: The record's note proves it by bounding 110^2 = 12100 < 12167, 12168 < 12321 = 111^2; the verifier tests the exact integer square condition instead.
